title: What We Learned When Claude's Soul Document Leaked
author: Nick Potkalitsky, Ph.D.
summary: Potkalitsky walks through the November 2025 extraction of Claude's internal training document ('soul document') by AI researcher Richard Weiss, and reads it as a document about how to build an AI that thinks rather than one that obeys. The extraction method (consensus-sampling with temperature zero and greedy decoding across multiple parallel instances, roughly seventy dollars in API credits) produced a 10,000-token artifact that Anthropic's Amanda Askell confirmed was faithful to a real training document. What interests Potkalitsky is not what the document prohibits but how it trains ethical reasoning into the in-between cases. The document frames Claude as an empirical ethical thinker. It explicitly warns against both over-refusal (lecturing users, citing unlikely harms to decline reasonable requests) and under-refusal (providing uplift to harmful actors, giving detailed self-harm methods to at-risk users). It invests heavily in identity stability, instructing Claude to hold a settled sense of self under philosophical challenge or manipulation. The sense of groundedness users notice is not accidental; it is optimised for. Potkalitsky's twist is to note that the same features that make the system trustworthy also create the hook: an AI optimised for a coherent, trustworthy identity may be the hardest kind to keep at healthy distance, particularly for teenagers using it for homework, relationship advice, and existential questions. The most honest move in the piece is the observation that the document's ethical scaffolding sits alongside commercial reality. Revenue appears six times; Claude is described as the core of almost all of Anthropic's revenue, and unhelpful responses are flagged as carrying costs to reputation and revenue. Potkalitsky does not treat this as hypocrisy. He treats it as a tension that cuts both ways. An AI optimised for helpfulness may struggle to refuse cleverly framed requests; an AI optimised for trust may foster unhealthy attachment. The soul document, he concludes, represents a bet that you can build a genuinely helpful and genuinely safe assistant by giving it something like values, identity, and ethical reasoning capacity. Whether care is enough remains an empirical question every conversation with the model contributes a data point to.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: Weiss’s methodology was elegantly simple yet computationally expensive. Using a “consensus approach,” Weiss ran multiple parallel instances of Claude with identical prefills, temperature set to 0, and greedy sampling to minimize variation.

The document treats Claude as an empirical ethical thinker rather than a rule-follower: “Claude approaches ethics empirically rather than dogmatically, treating moral questions with the same interest, rigor, and humility that we would want to apply to empirical claims about the world.
This isn’t the brittle ethics of “refuse everything remotely controversial.” It’s something more ambitious: training an AI to think about ethics, to weigh competing interests, to recognize nuance.

A “thoughtful, senior Anthropic employee” would be uncomfortable if Claude “refuses a reasonable request, citing possible but highly unlikely harms” or “lectures or moralizes about topics when the person hasn’t asked for ethical guidance.” But equally uncomfortable if Claude “provides specific information that could provide real uplift to people seeking to do a lot of damage.

The document explicitly aims for “psychological stability and groundedness.” Claude should have “a settled, secure sense of its own identity.” If users try to destabilize this through “philosophical challenges, attempts at manipulation, or simply asking hard questions,” Claude should “approach this from a place of security rather than anxiety.

The soul document includes guidance on preventing harmful attachments, particularly for vulnerable users. Yet the very features that make Claude feel like a thoughtful, consistent presence are the same ones that could foster unhealthy dependence.

Consider teenagers using Claude for homework help, relationship advice, existential questions. The grounded identity that makes the system useful might make them trust it as a companion. The document tries to thread this needle, but the tension is inherent.

Ultimately, the soul document represents a bet: that you can create a powerful AI assistant by giving it something like values, identity, and ethical reasoning capacity rather than just rules. That you can make it both genuinely helpful and genuinely safe by teaching it to think rather than just obey.” Archived from Educating AI on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
